title: The Slack app

story: Tuesday, 11:02. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, is building RH-1234 and reaches a question its plan does not answer. It posts in the ticket's Slack thread, "Should the empty card have a Create project button?", and waits; ten minutes later its VM is parked: stopped, with its disk kept, until the answer comes. At 11:05 the platform team deploys a new version of the Slack app, so the old process stops and a new one starts.

At 11:20 you reply in the thread: "Yes, the same button as in the header." A minute later you add: "And the text should say No projects yet." Suppose the old app had kept "this thread belongs to nova:RH-1234" in a variable. The new process has never heard of the thread, so both replies go nowhere. Nobody sees an error, and two days later Nova hands the ticket back because "nobody answered".
hook.question: How does every click, command and reply in Slack reach the right run, with the right person's name on it, when the Slack app itself can restart at any moment?

p: Three things take part: Slack, where people talk; the run nova:RH-1234 in Temporal, which waits for signals; and between them our Slack app, a small program built with Bolt, Slack's framework for apps, that translates between the two. Every ticket gets one thread in the Nova channel. Its first message is the status message, one line such as "RH-1234 · Nova: Needs info", and the run keeps it current with chat.update on the same message instead of posting a new one at every step. A Slack message is identified by its channel and its ts, a timestamp string like 1792135138.000001 that Slack gives every message, and a reply in a thread carries the first message's ts as its thread_ts.

The run keeps that ts in its own state, and the broker, the service that holds our Slack, GitHub and Jira credentials and makes those calls for each run, records the thread as part of the run's Slack scope, the list of places the run may post. That is also why Nova can post only into this one thread. From then on, everything people do can be traced back to the run from the event alone, plus at most one lookup. A button carries the workflow ID in its value. A reply carries thread_ts, and the broker's record says which run owns that thread. A command names the ticket, and the run's ID is nova:<ticket>. The app needs no memory of its own, because every event carries its address.

notes.text: Every signal says who did it, so Jira and the PR can record it. The mapping lives in a file in the repo, not in the app.
The app makes the Jira change with its own account, so Jira's history would not show who asked. This property records the person, and the poll reads it first when it looks for the requester.
/nova does not start a run itself. It hands the ticket over the same way a person does in Jira, so there is one door for new work and the requester is recorded in one way.
A query, answered by the worker from the run's current state. The app never keeps its own copy of the status.

deeper.h: Go deeper: Socket Mode and the three-second rule
p: The app runs in Socket Mode: it opens a WebSocket to Slack and receives events through it, so we publish no URL that anyone on the internet could call. It needs two tokens from Vault, the app token (xapp-) to open the socket and the bot token (xoxb-) to call Slack's Web API.

Slack waits at most three seconds for an acknowledgement, so every handler calls ack() first and only then talks to Temporal, Jira or Slack. You built both of these in the lesson about Slack apps with Bolt.

The Slack app is a process on our internal cluster, and processes there are replaced all the time: every deploy, every node that restarts, and during a rollout two copies run side by side for a moment. A value kept in a variable is lost on restart, and in a rollout one copy may know it while the other does not. That is exactly the bug from the story. So the app follows one rule, the same one as any stateless web service: every handler gets what it needs from the event itself, from the run, or from a durable record, and never from its own memory.

Here is the handler that turns a reply into an answer. It keeps only messages written by people inside a thread: no subtype, which would mean an edit, a join or another system message; no bot_id, which would mean a bot, Nova's own question included; and a thread_ts. Then it asks the broker which run owns the thread, on every message, and sends the answerQuestion signal with the text and who wrote it. Temporal stores the signal in the run's history at once, even if no worker is running at that moment, so once the signal call succeeds, the reply cannot be lost.

notes.text: Without the bot_id check, Nova's own question would arrive as an answer to itself.
Asked on every message. A copy cached when the app started would miss every thread opened after that.
An ephemeral message is one only that person can see.

p: People rarely answer in one message. You wrote two, a minute apart, and while Nova's parked VM wakes up a third could arrive. If the run's signal handler simply stored the latest text, the earlier replies would disappear, and Nova would build the card without the button. So the handler adds each reply to a list, and when the VM is awake the run joins the list, with who wrote each line, into the one message the session resumes with.

Decisions work the other way. A plan has exactly one decision, so after a click the app edits the message to say who decided and removes the buttons, and the run ignores any decision that arrives after it already has one. Replies are joined; decisions are taken once.

notes.text: The handler only records. The workflow body decides when to use the replies.
splice(0) takes every reply so far and empties the list, ready for the next question.

lab.title: Replies find their run
needs: The course repo at ~/Projects/ai-agents-course (the lab starts from the p7-4 lab's files)
lab.goal: Run a real Bolt app, a pretend Slack and a Temporal run on your laptop, and make a person's replies in a ticket's thread reach the right run as one joined answer, even across a restart of the app.

guess.q: Nova asked its question in RH-1234's thread, then the Slack app restarted. Now the requester replies. Where must the app look to find which run owns the thread?

options.text: In a Map the app filled when the question was posted
options.why: The Map died with the old process. The new process has an empty Map, so the reply goes nowhere.

options.text: In a durable record outside the app, read when the reply arrives
options.why: The broker recorded the thread when Nova posted in it. Any copy of the app, old or new, finds the same answer.

options.text: In the reply's text, which mentions the ticket key
options.why: People do not write ticket keys in their replies. The address is the thread, not the words.

lab.build: Write the message handler in app.mjs, following its comment: return early for a message with a subtype, a bot_id or no thread_ts; read threads.json (the broker's record) inside the handler; find the workflow ID for event.thread_ts; and signal answerQuestion with the text and people[event.user]. Restart the app (Ctrl+C, node app.mjs). Then play the thread: node slack.mjs bot "Should the empty card have a Create project button?" (Nova's own message, which must be ignored), then reply as U_SEAN, and within ten seconds reply again: node slack.mjs reply U_SEAN "And the text should say No projects yet." Last, prove the restart is harmless: node start.mjs for a new run, restart the app before you answer, and reply as U_DANA.
checks: The bot message produces no answerQuestion line in the third terminal.
The third terminal shows sean@example.com replied in the thread of nova:RH-1234 -> answerQuestion once per reply.
The second terminal shows Nova resumes the session with both replies from U_SEAN, each on its own line with the email sean@example.com.
temporal workflow result --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 shows both replies joined, and the status message ends as RH-1234 · Nova: PR open, edited in place (always the same ts).
With a restart of the app between the question and the answer, Dana's reply still reaches the new run.
lab.fix: A teammate moved the read of threads.json to the top of app.mjs, "so we don't read the file on every message". Make the same change (read it once into a const next to people), restart the app, start a new run with node start.mjs and reply as U_SEAN. The reply is acknowledged with 200, no answerQuestion line appears, and /nova status still says Needs info: the new thread was opened after the app read the file, so the app's copy has never heard of it. Read the record inside the handler again.
explain: Which three places may the Slack app get information from, and why never from its own variables?
Why does the handler skip messages with a bot_id, and what would happen without that check?
Why does the run join replies but take only the first decision on a plan?
lab.done: Two replies arrive in the run as one joined answer, a restart of the app loses nothing, and you stopped the app, the worker and the dev server with Ctrl+C.

check.q: The Slack app restarts between Nova's question and your reply. Which design still delivers the reply to nova:RH-1234?

options.text: The app keeps a Map from thread to run and saves it to the pod's local disk on shutdown
options.why: A new pod starts with a new disk, and during a rollout two copies run at once. Only a record outside the app is shared by all copies.

options.text: On every reply, the app asks the broker which run owns the reply's thread
options.why: The broker recorded the thread when Nova posted in it, so any copy of the app finds the same run.

options.text: The app asks the person to repeat their answer after every deploy
options.why: Nobody would know that a deploy happened, and the answer would still be lost until someone noticed.

check.q: Why does /nova RH-1234 assign the ticket to Nova instead of starting the run itself?

options.text: Because a Slack app is not allowed to call Temporal
options.why: The app does call Temporal, for status queries and for signals such as stop.

options.text: Because assigning is faster than starting a workflow
options.why: It is slower, since the poll needs up to a minute. Speed is not the reason.

options.text: Because then every hand-off goes through the Jira poll, which records the requester and applies the walls in one place
options.why: One door for new work: the same requester rule, the same one-run-per-ticket name and the same kill switch, whether you used Jira or Slack.

check.q: You answer Nova's question in two messages before Nova's VM is awake. What should the run hand to Nova?

options.text: Both replies joined, each with who wrote it
options.why: People answer in pieces. The handler appends every reply, and the run joins them when the session resumes.

options.text: Only the last reply, because it is the most recent
options.why: That is the overwrite bug: the first reply, the button, would be lost.

options.text: Only the first reply, because a question has one answer
options.why: That rule is for plan decisions, which are taken once. Answers to questions are joined.

p: The app lives in ai-agents/slack-app: src/app.ts with Bolt 5 in Socket Mode and the /nova command, and src/actions.ts with one app.action handler that maps every button to a signal, the change modal, and the message handler for replies. Its tokens come from Vault at infrastructure/ai-agents/slack-app. config/people.yaml maps Slack IDs to Jira accounts, GitHub logins and emails, and the broker records which run posted in which thread, which is also the run's Slack scope.

Details to settle while you build: G3-35 says replies are joined, but the answerQuestion handler in G3-24 overwrites, so use a list as in this lesson. G3-30 passes `by` as a person object and G3-35 as an email; pick one. G3-35 maps the backstop's Continue button to a resume signal that no workflow defines yet, and its button value format (nova:RH-1234|3) differs from G4-14's (nova:RH-1234|v2).

tickets.why: The Bolt app in Socket Mode, /nova start, status and stop, one status message per ticket.
Buttons and modals as signals with who did it, replies in the thread as answerQuestion.
/nova RH-1234 becomes "assign the ticket to Nova", and config/people.yaml.
What the plan message looks like, the version in the button value, and who may decide.

words.plain: Slack's ID of a message (a timestamp string), and, on a reply, the ts of the thread's first message.
The first message of a ticket's thread, edited in place with chat.update as the run moves.
An app that keeps nothing between requests; everything comes from the event, the run or a durable record.
The signal a person's reply in the thread becomes, carrying the text and who wrote it.
A Slack message only one person can see, used to tell them something went wrong.

review.q: From memory: how a button click, a reply in the thread and a /nova command each find their run.
review.a: A button carries the workflow ID in its value. A reply carries thread_ts, and the broker's record says which run owns that thread. A command names the ticket, and the run is nova:<ticket>.

review.q: A teammate caches the thread record when the app starts "to save a call". What breaks, and when?
review.a: Every thread opened after the app started is unknown, so replies there are silently ignored until the next restart. Read the record on every message.

review.q: Why does the status message use chat.update instead of a new message per step?
review.a: One message per ticket stays readable and always shows the current state; its ts is stored in the run, so any copy of the app or worker can edit it.

remember: The Slack app remembers nothing: every event carries its address, and the run and the broker hold the rest.
